newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW - NZD to keep rising - Zurich Investment.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - NZD to keep rising - Zurich Investment.

text.p: The New Zealand dollar will continue its upward climb over the next six to 12 months, Zurich Investment Management managing director Gordon Johns said on Wednesday.
In an interview with Reuters at the New Zealand Investment Conference in Auckland, Johns said it was hard to see the currency deteriorating over 1997.

"It's very difficult to make point forecasts about these things, but all other things being equal, I would say yes, I would expect the Kiwi dollar to be stronger. Hugely stronger, no, but somewhat stronger, yes, on a TWI (Trade-Weighted Index) basis and against the U.S. dollar, which is really what counts."

Johns said Zurich Investment Management's view of New Zealand as a "very solid story" had been confirmed during the conference, which has been addressed by key politicians, economists, and Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Don Brash.

"The fact is, you've got a damn good story here. You've got a government pursuing basically the right policies, you've got an economy which is healthy, a private sector doing the right things, and under those circumstances it's very difficult to see the currency depreciate," he said.
"There are identifiable clouds which are, primarily, as Don Brash said -- the possibility that the interest rate differential may not be so much in New Zealand's favour, and also the current account.
"Nonetheless, there is still an awful lot in New Zealand's favour. We still come up with the New Zealand dollar as being one of the most attractive currencies in the world."
Johns said it would be very difficult for the RBNZ to achieve its preferred mix of monetary conditions. Brash has recently reiterated that he would prefer a lower currency and higher interest rates.

"I rather detected a feeling that there wasn't much support among anybody else here (at the conference) for the feeling that interest rates really needed to be higher, that it's very much Brash's obsession because a la Greenspan he is worried about
irrational exuberance in the Auckland property market," Johns said.

"That's perfectly reasonable, but I'm not sure that justifies high short term interest rates if you look at the economy as a whole. On any international comparison, this country looks in pretty good shape. It really does."

Johns said he saw growth as one of the most important determinants of currency direction, and growth forecasts were in New Zealand's favour. Even the prospect of underlying inflation at the top of the central bank's 0-3 percent target band was no major impediment to offshore investment.
"It may not be as wonderful as some of the expectations, but we've still got the prospect, even with extra spending and slippage fiscally, of government surpluses for the next several years."
Johns said Zurich Investment saw interest rate differentials between New Zealand and the rest of the world narrowing modestly over the next six to 12 months.

"But the one thing you have to say about the New Zealand economy and the New Zealand currency is you are more vulnerable than most others because you are a relatively small economy in terms of absolute size, and you are a very undiversified economy
in terms of the mix...of production and exports.
"That makes you a relatively volatile and relatively high- risk economy and currency and there's nothing you can ever do about that." -- Wellington newsroom (64 4) 473 4746
